claims.text: The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a uniform fcc matrix.
The as-built alloy contains minimal pre-existing oxide.
High-temperature degradation in oxidizing environments is controlled by selective oxidation of chromium and titanium.
Selective oxidation produces a mixed, sub-stoichiometric Cr–Ti oxide scale at the fcc-matrix interface.
The initially formed Cr–Ti oxide scale is continuous and protective.
Prolonged exposure causes the oxide scale to thicken.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the oxide scale and fcc substrate generates interfacial stresses.
Interfacial stresses cause microcracking and eventual delamination of the oxide scale.
Microcracking and delamination of the oxide scale lead to mechanical degradation.
At 800°C for 100 hours in air, the alloy will develop a continuous mixed Cr–Ti oxide layer.
The oxide layer formed in air will exhibit microcracking and partial spallation.
Exposure in air will reduce strength or fatigue resistance relative to the as-built state.
A 95% Ar–5% H2 atmosphere suppresses oxidation relative to air.
Under the reducing atmosphere, an oxide scale will either not form or remain very thin.
Under the reducing atmosphere, the original microstructure and mechanical integrity will be largely preserved.
The proposed mechanism is applicable around 800°C, for exposure durations on the order of 100 hours, when comparing clearly oxidizing and reducing gases.
At substantially different temperatures or durations, additional degradation mechanisms may operate.
Minor processing variations may change oxide-scale failure, microcracking, spallation, and mechanical degradation.
